title: Inside an Atom
subtitle: The nucleus out to the seventh electron shell
sourceNote: Bohr radii (n squared times 52.9 pm). Shell radii are a simplified model, but the numbers are real.

waypoints.name: The edge of the nucleus
waypoints.body: That is the whole nucleus behind you already. It holds virtually all the atom's mass in about a millionth of its width. Everything ahead is essentially empty.

waypoints.name: The first shell
waypoints.body: The Bohr radius, 52.9 picometres. This is where hydrogen's single electron is most likely to be found. It is sixty thousand times further out than the nucleus edge.

waypoints.name: The second shell
waypoints.body: Four times further out than the first. Shells grow as the square of their number, so each one is a bigger jump than the last.

waypoints.name: The third shell
waypoints.body: Sodium, magnesium and the rest of the third row keep their outermost electrons about here.

waypoints.name: The fourth shell
waypoints.body: Where the transition metals begin. Iron, copper and zinc all do their chemistry from roughly this distance out.

waypoints.name: The fifth shell
waypoints.body: Silver and tin territory. The atom is now twenty-five times wider than the first shell, and still almost entirely empty space.

waypoints.name: The sixth shell
waypoints.body: Gold, mercury and lead. Electrons out here move fast enough that relativity starts to matter, which is why gold looks yellow.

waypoints.name: The seventh shell
waypoints.body: The outer edge, where uranium and the heaviest elements keep their last electrons. You have crossed an atom, and nearly all of it was nothing at all.
